The cost of consumer credit is rising.

The average interest rate on a US credit card rose +0.2 percentage points in August, to 22.36%, its highest level in 12 months.

This is now only 1.0 percentage point below the record 23.37% set in August 2024.

Since 2021, the average credit card interest rate has surged +6.5 percentage points.

By comparison, the 5-year average before the 2020 pandemic was 14.94%.

Meanwhile, the average interest rate on a 5-year new car loan rose +0.4 percentage points in August, to 7.54%, its highest since August 2025.

This is 3.5 percentage points above pre-pandemic levels, but 0.9 percentage points below its all-time high of 8.4%, recorded in August 2024.

Consumer borrowing has rarely been this expensive.

tweets.text:
AI will become one of the largest spending categories in the US economy:

AI services are projected to account for a record 8.8% of US GDP in 2032.

This estimate shows how much businesses and consumers are expected to spend per year on the services of AI companies.

This also implies AI companies would generate ~$3.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2032.

By comparison, US consumer spending on food accounts for a similar 9.1% of GDP.

This figure would also be ~72% higher than energy, at 5.1% of GDP, and twice the size of construction as well as computers and software, both at 4.4%.

It would also be nearly 3x defense, at 2.8%, and more than 7x communications and internet, at 1.2% of GDP.

The only category where spending is significantly larger is health, at 18% of GDP.

The scale of the AI revolution is unlike anything seen before.

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida on why the boring SaaS companies are best positioned to win AI:

Ben: "When the coding agents came out, it was the SaaSpocalypse, and all their values dropped through the floor. Then when Jev came out, every SaaS company is like, 'This is the greatest thing ever.'"

Diogo: "In the SaaSpocalypse story, the story I feel has panned out really poorly is that software is very cheap and perhaps easy to replicate. I could believe the former. I could not believe the latter, because a lot of the stuff happens beneath the hood."

"I think SaaS will be one of the largest winners of the whole AI game."

"I want to work really, really well with the biggest, most boring SaaS companies because I think they're the best positioned to know what workflows to automate, what people need. That's their bread and butter."

"I'm not going to forecast anything about the financial markets. But as far as capabilities go, I think it's going to be like an inverse SaaSpocalypse. I'm so jazzed about it."

BREAKING: China’s central bank officially bought +23 tonnes of gold in September, its largest monthly purchase since September 2023.

This follows +20 tonnes purchased in both August and July, and marks its 23rd consecutive monthly gold purchase.

So far in 2026, China has officially acquired +103 tonnes of gold, raising total holdings to a record 2,410 tonnes.

China is now the world’s 5th-largest gold holder, following the US, Germany, Italy, and France.

At this pace, it could surpass Italy and France as early as this year, which hold 2,452 tonnes and 2,437 tonnes, respectively.

China is aggressively buying the dip in gold.

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida on why Jev is called Jev, and what cheap intelligence finally changes about software:

"It's wild that AI is so cool and software has been unchanged in 10 years... The most we can do is add a little chatbot in the side sometimes that can take actions, but not all actions."

"TypeSafe is making AI for software. We want to make AI powerful, not just for humans in the loop, but to actually build real software."

"It's about the laziness to spend 10 hours to do the five-minute task instantly and to never have to do it again. It should be an ROI decision for people who automate stuff. I would just like it to be automatable."

"I think that people will just make new kinds of work, hence the Jev in Jevons. New kinds of work once that stuff is doable."

"As we have lots of intelligence at lots of different cost and speed trade-offs, the super systems-y types will be making trade-offs. Jev's gonna be 1000x too smart for them. They just want an approximate guess to optimistically route here and there."

Martin Casado: "The good news is we get to rebuild systems again. We have a new primitive. It's kind of a new way of thinking about doing software."

@CompleteSkeptic @typesafeai @bhorowitz @martin_casado

History says this is the best quarter of the entire four-year cycle for US stocks.

Since 1950, the S&P 500's average fourth-quarter return in a midterm election year is about 6.6%, far above the roughly 2.5% to 4% in the other three years of a presidential term. 2026 is a midterm year.

France is getting downgraded by every major rating agency at once, and the reason is a deficit it cannot control.

France has blown through the EU's 3% deficit limit every year for the better part of a decade. It hit 9% of GDP in 2020 and still runs around 5.5%, and the government's big new plan is to get the deficit down to 5% by 2027. They are calling that progress.

All five agencies, Fitch, Moody's, S&P Global, DBRS and Scope, have cut France, several of them below AA for the first time in modern history. Bond prices are down about 15% over the past six years. Total return is close to flat. That gap is the entire lesson in owning bonds right now.

As yields marched to multi-decade highs, the price of this Treasury fund fell around 15%. But the income it threw off the whole way nearly erased that loss on a total-return basis.

In a high-yield world, the coupon does the heavy lifting. If you own bonds for the income and hold to the cash flows, a lower price is noise. If you bought a bond fund betting the price snaps back, you may be waiting a long time. Know which one you are.

After a wondrous first half for investors, especially for those in growth stocks, the second half of 2026 has been a struggle.  The Russell 3,000 -- which represents roughly 98% of publicly traded US stock market cap -- is up about 3% in the 2nd half, but the average stock in the index is actually down 4.4%.

Along with rising interest rates hurting the most interest-rate sensitive areas of the market, it appears as if the shorts are betting big and winning these days.

We broke the Russell 3,000 into deciles (10 groups of roughly 300 stocks each) based on each stock's short interest as a percentage of its equity float.  We then calculated the average 2nd half percentage change of the stocks in each decile.

Decile one in the chart below all the way to the left of the image, contains the decile of most heavily shorted stocks in the Russell 3,000.  Stocks in this decile are down an average of 13.6% in the 2nd half.  As short interest levels get smaller, performance gets better, and the two deciles containing the least heavily shorted stocks are actually averaging gains in the 2nd half.

During big market rallies, shorts feel the pain and usually push prices higher as they rush to cover.  We're definitely not in that type of environment now, and we haven't been for months.

On the flip side, as the shorts get more confident from their winning ways, the spring gets coiled further.  The next time we get a positive market development that brings investors back into equities, be it from lower oil prices, lower rates, upside earnings, economic surprises, or something that's not on anyone's radar right now, the ensuing short covering could be more extreme than usual.

For now, though, the shorts are winning big in the second half.

Large-cap growth just did something that has always led higher a year later.

After a six-month decline, IWF turned around and posted a six-month gain of 20% or more, a price thrust that fired on September 28. In 20-plus years, every prior case was followed by higher large-cap prices, and 6 of the 9 completed signals gained 10% or more over the next year.

This week's TradingEdge Weekly video covers the growth thrust, transportation and real estate seasonality, a credit spread divergence near the highs, and breadth pressure spilling into emerging markets.
